slides.title: Grow instead of search?
slides.subtitle: Function-preserving depth growth vs. depth search for multi-task PPO on Meta-World MT10
slides.footer: COMP9501 Advanced Machine Learning  ·  43 runs  ·  5 seeds
slides.notes: If you do not know how deep your policy should be, can you grow it during one run instead of training several networks and picking the best?

slides.title: Choosing depth usually means training K networks
slides.takeaway: Can one growing run match a searched depth at lower total cost?
slides.notes: The usual answer to an unknown depth is search: one run per candidate depth, keep the best on validation. That multiplies the cost of RL training by K. Growth starts shallow and adds layers inside one run.

slides.title: An identity layer adds depth without changing the policy
stats: new layer starts as identity after a ReLU
slides.takeaway: Existing weights and optimiser state are kept; only the new layer starts fresh
slides.source: Pilot: 3 tasks, 1 seed, 60 held-out episodes. Light bars: at insertion; dark bars: +300k steps.
slides.notes: We append a square linear layer initialised to the identity, followed by a ReLU. Its input is already non-negative, so the output is unchanged and the policy is identical at insertion. Existing weights keep their Adam state; the critic is untouched. In a pilot, a random layer collapsed success to zero, the identity layer changed nothing.

slides.title: Ten robot tasks, goal positions held out from training
rows: Meta-World MT10, one policy for 10 tasks
slides.takeaway: Only actor depth and growth timing vary between runs
slides.notes: Every run uses the same PPO recipe and three million environment steps. Each task has fifty goal variants: thirty for training, ten for model selection, ten held out. All numbers we report are on held-out goals.

slides.title: Growth against search, and against guessing
slides.takeaway: Cost counts every environment step spent before a final model is chosen
slides.notes: Grid search trains all four depths and picks by validation success. Successive halving trains all four to 0.5M steps, keeps two to 1.5M and one to 3M; we simulate it from the same logged curves. Default and random depth commit without search. The growth runs start at depth one and add two layers.

slides.title: Held-out goals are as easy as training goals
stats: gap between training and held-out goals
slides.takeaway: Goal variants interpolate within a task; the split does not add difficulty
slides.notes: Across every configuration, held-out success is within a few points of training-goal success. The held-out split is a valid test, but on MT10 it does not make the problem harder.

slides.title: Depth matters
slides.takeaway: The wrong depth costs up to 24 points
slides.notes: One hidden layer plateaus in the mid sixties; four layers reach 88 percent. The best depth is three for two seeds and four for three, so it is worth choosing well.

slides.title: Depth pays off on the harder manipulation tasks
slides.takeaway: Gains come from peg-insert, push and drawer-open; easy tasks are solved at any depth
slides.notes: Held-out success per task, mean of five seeds. Six tasks are solved at every depth. The differences come from peg insertion, pushing and drawer opening. Pick-and-place stays hard for every configuration within this budget.

slides.title: Growing runs never dip at insertion
slides.takeaway: Early growth catches up with deep networks; late growth runs out of time
slides.notes: Each line is one seed; dotted lines are insertions. No insertion changed the policy and no curve drops afterwards. Growing early leaves two million steps at full depth and catches up; growing late leaves one million and ends near depth two.

slides.title: Grow early ≈ successive halving, for one run
slides.takeaway: Same accuracy as cheap search at 55% of the steps; 5 points below the best depth
slides.notes: Paired over five seeds. Growing early reaches 84 percent with one run, about the same as successive halving with 5.5 million steps, and better than a default or random depth. Grid search finds the best depth, 89 percent, at four times the cost.

slides.title: GPU time does not track compute at this model size
slides.takeaway: We compare cost in environment steps and FLOPs
slides.notes: Learner FLOPs grow with depth, but GPU time barely changes and varies with server load: these networks are small enough that kernel launch overhead dominates. So cost is reported in environment steps and FLOPs. In FLOPs, grow early uses a quarter of grid search.

slides.title: With a narrow actor, growth does not help
slides.takeaway: The benefit depends on width and schedule (2 seeds)
slides.notes: With width 128, growing to depth three stays below even a random depth. Only two seeds, so we read it as a warning sign, not a conclusion.

slides.title: Takeaways
points: Identity insertion grows a policy safely
No change at insertion, no dip afterwards
Grow early ≈ cheap search for one run
84% vs 85%, still below the best depth (89%)
slides.footer: Scope: one benchmark · 5 seeds · fixed growth schedules.   Next: plateau-triggered growth, MT50.
slides.notes: Three messages: growth is safe, depth matters, and growing early gives cheap-search performance for one run, but not best-depth performance. Next we would trigger growth on a plateau and test on MT50.
